title: Nasdaq Slides, Tech Sell‑Off Returns; Oil Crashes on U.S.–Iran Diplomacy Hopes (Nov 2, 2026)
body:
Wall Street opened the week on a cautious note on Monday, as the Nasdaq Composite slipped back into the red after a brief rally in early trading, while the broader market posted a mixed bag of results. The decline was driven primarily by a renewed sell‑off in high‑growth technology names that had briefly reclaimed some of their early‑session momentum. At the same time, crude oil prices tumbled sharply, falling more than 4% on renewed optimism that diplomatic overtures could finally de‑escalate the protracted conflict between the United States and Iran, a development that has long weighed on energy markets.

The Nasdaq’s 0.7% drop erased most of the gains it had logged the previous day, with the index closing at 15,842, down from a recent intraday high of 16,010. Heavyweights such as Nvidia, Meta Platforms, and Amazon led the retreat, each shedding between 1.5% and 2.8% after reporting weaker‑than‑expected earnings guidance or flagging slower demand for cloud and advertising services. By contrast, the S&P 500 managed a modest 0.2% rise, buoyed by strength in industrials and consumer staples, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average inched up 0.1% on the back of solid performance from legacy manufacturers and utilities.

Energy markets reacted to a very different set of catalysts. Brent crude slid to $78.45 per barrel, its lowest level since early August, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate fell to $74.30, marking the steepest one‑day decline in three weeks. Traders cited a series of diplomatic signals that suggest a possible cease‑fire agreement could be on the horizon. Earlier in the day, senior officials from the State Department disclosed that back‑channel talks between Washington and Tehran had resumed, focusing on a framework for a phased withdrawal of U.S. forces from the Gulf region. The news lifted risk appetite among investors, prompting a shift away from the safe‑haven appeal of oil and into equities, albeit selectively.

Analysts note that the tech sell‑off reflects a broader recalibration of expectations for growth stocks after a year of extraordinary valuations. “Investors are starting to price in the reality that the macro environment—higher rates, tighter credit, and lingering supply‑chain constraints—will temper the explosive growth we saw in 2023 and 2024,” said Maya Patel, senior equity strategist at Meridian Capital. “The sector is not collapsing, but the exuberance is fading, and we’re seeing a rotation toward more defensively positioned companies.”

Meanwhile, the oil market’s bounce back from a prolonged slump underscores how geopolitical risk premiums can still dominate pricing dynamics. “Even a modest signal that the U.S. and Iran might be moving toward a diplomatic solution can shave several dollars off a barrel,” explained Carlos Mendes, energy analyst at Global Commodities Research. “If a formal agreement is reached, we could see a further 5%‑10% correction in crude prices over the next month, which would have ripple effects across energy‑intensive industries and emerging market economies that rely on cheap oil imports.”

Looking ahead, market participants will be watching several key data points for clues on the direction of both equities and commodities. The U.S. consumer price index slated for release later this week will test the Federal Reserve’s stance on interest rates, while the upcoming International Energy Agency report on global oil demand will gauge whether the diplomatic optimism is already translating into tangible shifts in consumption patterns. In the tech arena, earnings season is far from over, with several megacap firms slated to report later this month, providing further insight into whether the sector’s recent weakness is a temporary correction or a more sustained slowdown.

If diplomatic progress continues and the Fed signals a more dovish policy path, the mixed performance seen on Monday could give way to a broader rally, especially in sectors that have been lagging behind the energy recovery. Conversely, any setbacks in the U.S.–Iran talks or a surprise hawkish move by the Fed could reignite volatility, pulling both tech stocks and oil prices back into defensive territory. Investors will therefore need to balance the twin narratives of geopolitical easing and macro‑economic tightening as they navigate the market’s next moves.
